Ask HN: What in the world is taking Ubuntu so long?
candidates.text: Ubuntu has CVE-2026-98432 marked as a 9.8, but yet it's coming up on a week with no update to fix it. It's still marked as "work in progress" (though at least now they've listed a mitigation): https://ubuntu.com/security/CVE-2026-98432 I've had mitigations in place for a week, but this response is really shaking my confidence in Ubuntu. I'm just trying to understand what is going on with Ubuntu. Do they have too many kernels (that page is loooong), do they not have enough automation in the build/test pipeline, are their engineers overwhelmed? We are moving into a world where there are going to be vastly more security issues; if you can't keep up now, where are you going to be in the next 6 months? For a long time keeping on top of OS updates has been a huge part of keeping the attackers at bay. However, the world is changing.

candidates.title: Pinpointing Location of Videos from Background Airplane Sounds
candidates.text: This is fascinating : The video describes a technique that can reveal where an otherwise unidentifiable recording was made by analyzing its audio for the faint sounds of passing aircraft. The technique is both fascinating and frightening. It works by looking at Doppler curves, which plot the way a plane’s sound changes as it passes overhead because of the Doppler effect. This is the same familiar Doppler effect that causes the frequency of a siren to rise as it approaches and then fall as it passes by and moves away. More generally, it’s the phenomenon whereby the frequency of a wave perceived by an observer changes when the observer and the source of the wave are moving in relation to one another...

candidates.title: After Binance, check what your signing systems can approve
candidates.text: Binance’s October 2026 security incident raises an operational question for every organization holding user funds: Can your security controls recognize when a valid signature grants an attacker wallet authority? If an organization only monitors transfers and ownership changes, it may miss the shift in wallet authority until assets move. Binance’s initial update about the incident suggested that a compromised DevOps laptop allowed an attacker to access a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawals. Its second update reported additional breaches but no evidence that wallet private keys had leaked. In its November 3 report , Binance described a broader attack involving social engineering, misuse of an internal AI tool, stolen credentials, and unauthorized access to its wallet-signing service. The attacker nevertheless obtained valid signatures, illustrating a major risk: a compromised server with permission to request signatures can misuse a protected key without extracting it. The attacker used an EIP-7702 delegation that allows a wallet to sign a standing instruction: “Use this code when my account is called.” Ethereum keeps that instruction in place until it is changed or cleared using the wallet’s key. That enabled repeated transfers , including funds deposited after the first theft, without further signatures from Binance. Other Binance wallets were drained through ordinary signed transfers. Transaction execution and monitoring systems must keep pace with Ethereum

Show HN: Coldframe, a honeypot that poses as a supermarket fridge controller
candidates.text: I built Coldframe, a honeypot that pretends to be a supermarket refrigeration controller. Inspired by the events on industrial fridge installations in the past weeks, I wanted to see what people would try against a convincing fake. To learn more about this I built a honeypot that resembled perfectly the Danfoss AK-SM 800A and Dixell XWEB interfaces. Both of them are recognized on Shodan as real ones (an not as honeypots). It’s one Python file using only the standard library, and it builds on eppser/danfoss-ak-sm-decoy and public research by Synacktiv, Claroty and Ironhackers. Things that were fun to get right: - Matching real units. I used Shodan records of real devices to match header order, page titles, certificate fields and TLS versions. The Danfoss persona sends nginx headers in the same order as a real AK-SM 800A. The Dixell persona sends no Server header and pads its page to exactly 8,202 bytes. - Recognising exploit attempts. It recognises CVE-2025-41450, the Danfoss “code of the day” login bypass, and records whether the submitted code is correct for today. It also tags attempts targeting three other Danfoss CVEs and the XWEB vulnerabilities. - Letting them in. Default logins open a fake store dashboard with defrost buttons, so you see the second move, not just the first. Nothing behind it is real. Two instances have been live for a day. So far they’ve only seen generic scanners and Shodan’s crawler, which is called refrigerator.census.shodan.io. Feedback welcome, es

candidates.text: I love open-source software and open protocols, but my family and friends primarily communicate through SMS for exactly the reasons in https://xkcd.com/2365/ Whenever XMPP or Matrix threads pop up on HN, several commenters casually mention their "friends and family XMPP (or Matrix) server." How did you convince friends and family to move away from SMS/WhatsApp and replace it with a niche messaging app? My family and friends aren't hardcore nerdy, but they're more tech-savvy than average. Their needs in messaging are mainly pragmatic: they want ease of use, reliability, and fun features. They don't care that much about privacy, decentralization, or extensibility (though I care about those things a lot). I've been experimenting with self-hosting XMPP and Matrix servers and clients in the past week, and the UX is even worse than I expected. It seems like all the clients either imitate Slack, imitate Discord, or imitate hot garbage. I haven't seen any that try to be a simple, friendly replacement for SMS. I'm a software developer who uses computers all day, and I find the UX for most of the clients incredibly hard to use. The only angle I could see to pitch XMPP/Matrix to people for non-philosophical reasons are that there's a more consistent experience across iOS/Android. candidates.title: datasette #3046: Don't serve link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages
candidates.text: datasette #3046: Don't serve link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages I was looking at the Firefox network panel today when I noticed that requests to a Datasette table page were triggering an HTTP prefetch to the next page of rows in that table. This was happening because Datasette pages serve an HTTP link header like this: link: <https://latest.datasette.io/fixtures/compound_three_primary_keys?_next=a%2Cd%2Cv>; rel="next" This is bad. A tiny fraction of the visitors to one of those pages will click the "next" link, which means their browser is fetching unnecessary data and the Datasette server is having to render an entire page that then gets thrown away. I dug in and learned that Firefox has an issue that has been open for 24 years about this behavior... And one of the early comments on that issue links to my blog post from 2002 complaining about this feature. I hadn't just forgotten that I had written about it, I had forgotten the feature entirely! Tags: firefox , html , mozilla , datasette
